Neonatal Cayenne caecilians emerge from their egg capsule at a modest size; measurements from captive births indicate that newborns attain a total length at birth of 1.7 centimeters [Lb = 1.7 centimeters], a value consistent with the altricial state of many direct-developing caecilians. This initial length is soon left behind as the aquatic larvae begin a period of rapid somatic growth. The larval phase culminates in metamorphosis, a critical developmental transition that in this species occurs precisely when the individual reaches a total length at metamorphosis of 13.68 centimeters . This milestone coincides with the young caecilian leaving its mother, marking the onset of an independent, free-living existence. At this juncture, the newly metamorphosed juvenile possesses a wet weight at metamorphosis of only 6 grams , a figure that underscores the substantial energetic investment yet required to achieve adult proportions. This modest body mass at the larval–juvenile transition is typical of viviparous caecilians, which produce relatively small but developmentally advanced offspring.

The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in the size threshold for reproductive maturation. Females reach the onset of puberty at a total length at puberty for females of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters], whereas males begin their reproductive development at a smaller size, attaining puberty at 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters] in total length. This sex-specific difference in maturation size is reflected in the corresponding body masses at this developmental stage. Using allometric relationships derived from field-collected specimens, the wet weight at puberty for a female of this length is estimated at approximately 34.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 34.6 grams]. The earlier maturation of males at a smaller body size is a common pattern among caecilians and is typically interpreted as a strategy to maximize reproductive opportunities in a polygynous or scramble-competition mating system. Reaching puberty represents a significant physiological milestone, as it marks the completion of the juvenile growth phase and the onset of gametogenesis.

Under controlled thermal conditions, the time elapsed from metamorphosis to the attainment of sexual maturity has been quantified. The period spanning the post-metamorphic juvenile stage until puberty is 488 days following metamorphosis [tp = 488 days following metamorphosis] at 29 °C [T = 29 °C], a duration that reflects the protracted growth trajectory of this aquatic caecilian. During this sub-adult phase, individuals substantially increase both in length and in mass, accumulating the somatic resources necessary to support future reproductive effort. A gravid female measuring 42 centimeters in total length provides a useful reference point for adult body composition; such an individual, with a snout–vent length of 42 centimeters, typically exhibits a wet weight of 95 grams  at 42 centimeters total length, a mass achieved well after the attainment of puberty, as the female continues to add somatic tissue and fat reserves during the early part of her reproductive lifespan.

The ultimate total length attained by this species has been recorded at 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], a value that represents the asymptotic size approached by the largest adults in natural populations. At this maximum body length, predicted ultimate wet weight reaches 213 grams [Wwi = 213 grams], based on allometric scaling from the 42-centimeter reference female. Males tend to reach a slightly smaller final size; a male of 41.5 centimeters total length, for example, has a recorded wet weight of 84 grams  at 41.5 centimeters total length, illustrating the modest sexual size dimorphism present in this caecilian. The complete larval development period, from hatching to metamorphosis, spans approximately 183 days  at 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. The maximum reproductive rate for this species, expressed in a natural formulation, involves females producing between 6 and 14 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 6 and 14 eggs per clutch], with each female typically producing only one clutch every other year [F_R_i = one clutch every other year]. Although up to 14 eggs may be yolked, generally only 4 young successfully leave the mother.

Longevity records for the Cayenne caecilian, based on captive observations at a stable temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years], though this figure may be an overestimate relative to wild populations where predation and environmental stochasticity likely truncate survival. The relatively protracted generation time, coupled with the biennial reproductive cycle, aligns with the species’ placement along a slow life-history continuum. Comparative data from the related Mexican burrowing caecilian Dermophis mexicanus indicate that its hatchlings emerge from the egg membrane at a total length of 15 to 20 millimeters, a much smaller size that reflects its oviparous reproductive mode. In contrast, the viviparous Typhlonectes compressicauda produces larger neonates that are already relatively advanced at birth, a pattern consistent with its greater investment in each offspring. The interplay between a small clutch size and a prolonged interval between successive reproductive attempts reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a relatively low metabolic rate in this aquatic typhlonectid, a pattern commonly observed in caecilians that inhabit stable, resource-limited environments.
